fields.Front: In Internet jargon, what are the billions of connected computing devices at the edge of the network called?
fields.Back: Hosts, also called end systems. The two terms are interchangeable. They run (host) the network applications.

fields.Front: What does a packet switch do, and what are the two main types?
fields.Back: It forwards packets (chunks of data) from an incoming link to an outgoing link. The two main types are routers (network core) and link-layer switches (access networks).

fields.Front: Name four physical media used for communication links.
fields.Back: Fiber, copper (twisted pair), coaxial cable, radio (and satellite).

fields.Front: What is the transmission rate of a link also called, and in what units is it measured?
fields.Back: Bandwidth (or link capacity), measured in bits per second (bps).

fields.Front: In the nuts-and-bolts view, what is a 'network'?
fields.Back: A collection of devices, routers and links managed by a single organization (home, enterprise, mobile, datacenter, content-provider, or ISP network).

fields.Text: The Internet is often described in three words as a {{c1::network of networks}}: interconnected ISPs, nobody owns it.

fields.Front: Which organization develops Internet standards, and what are its standards documents called?
fields.Back: The IETF (Internet Engineering Task Force); its documents are RFCs (Requests for Comments).

fields.Text: Internet standards documents are called {{c1::RFCs (Requests for Comments)}} and are produced by the {{c2::IETF (Internet Engineering Task Force)}}.

fields.Front: Describe the 'service view' of the Internet in one sentence.
fields.Back: The Internet is an infrastructure that provides services to distributed applications (Web, email, games, streaming...) and offers a programming interface (hooks / sockets) with service options, analogous to a postal service.
